title: Learning Knowledge - 2
author: Martin Skelton
summary: This post traces how factual knowledge is learned through the four states Skelton uses: new, consolidating, treading water and drowning. Using a personal story about forgetting a new acquaintance's name, he shows new knowledge is tenuous until repeated experiences make it sticky. Hooks, such as his mnemonic for remembering the name, and rapid, short, repeated retrieval, as in Duolingo, move knowledge into the consolidating state. Treading water wastes time when learners already know the content, and drowning appears when pressure and nerves collapse recall, as in a game show and his own school exam. He sums up that knowledge learning involves choosing what to learn and many brief repeated experiences.
points: New knowledge is fragile and needs repeated experience, so a single encounter will not make it stick.
Each repeated knowledge experience can be very short, which means teachers can build stickiness in many twenty-second moments across a day.
Treading water is rewarding but wasteful when students already know the material, and teaches them that their existing knowledge does not count.
Drowning occurs when anxiety or humiliation overwhelms recall, so exam pressure and embarrassing teachers make knowledge learning worse.
Curriculum should decide which knowledge is learned at which age, because not everything can be made sticky.
quotes: Welcome to the ‘new’ stage of learning knowledge. The knowledge equivalent of those early sounds on the saxophone. Sort of close but not close enough, not correct and definitely not sticky.

It’s why my generation spent so much time daily chanting multiplication tables all those years ago. It’s why I can now hear 7 x 6 and, automatically, say 42. The endlessly repeated experiences made 7 x 6 = 42 very sticky indeed.

Knowledge learning follows the same path as other kinds of learning but the time for each repeated experience can be very short. As we shall see later, this matters a lot. It matters because, like Duolingo, we can help students make their knowledge sticky during multiple moments across each day, twenty seconds at a time.

In classes, students might be learning that their teacher doesn’t care about what they already know but cares more about what she wants to tell them. They might learn, over time, that they don’t matter as much as she does.
Eventually, still with songs to go, and very little money left to be won, they both burst into tears and gave up. They were drowning.

In schools, it’s the curriculum that should make this choice. A good curriculum helps by making it clear that in Grade 4 ‘this’ is the knowledge that children need to learn about plants but that in Grade 8, however, they now need to know ‘this’ much.
